newsitem.title: USA: CBOT July soybeans may have one more shot at $9/bu.
newsitem.headline: CBOT July soybeans may have one more shot at $9/bu.

text.p: Tight deliverable soybean stocks may send the volatile July contract back above $9.00 per bushel despite an increase in the U.S. Agriculture Department's ending soybean stocks forecast, analysts said.

"We started out the week with pretty heavy stocks in deliverable positions," said Dave Maher, analyst with Securities Corp of Iowa. "We woke up (Thursday) morning and all of a sudden there weren't any. I think on the old crop we'll work back up into the $8.60-$8.80 level and maybe test $9.00 by the time July goes off the board."
The U.S. Agriculture Department eased supply concerns only slightly on Thursday when it raised 1996-97 (Sept/Aug) ending stocks to 130 million bushels from 125 million.

"130 million is still an extremely tight situation and there's some question about how many beans are actually out there," said Jerry Gidel, Chicago-based analyst with Dean Witter. "We're still going to be volatile over the next three to four weeks until we get a better view of the crop."
The supply tightness was highlighted by a drop in soybean registrations. Deliverable grade soybean stocks fell to 20,000 bushels on Thursday from 580,000 the previous day.

Meanwhile, open interest in the July contract was estimated by CBOT at roughly 293 million bushels as of Thursday's close, leading many to speculate that no deliveries will be posted against the July.

Support for any rally "is going to come from the deliverable stocks issue," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Iowa. His price outlook for the July contract was $8.75 to $8.80 per bushel.
Roose also noted that open interest should fall next week ahead of the expiration of July options contracts on June 20.
"Next Friday, options go off the board," Roose said. "After that (speculators) are pretty much on their own. There is no insurance policy anymore."
Dean Witter's Gidel said the July could test the $9.02 contract high and the July/November spread could trade as high as $2.20. The spread peaked just under $2.00 this year.

"You might get the spread up to $2.20, with $9.00 in the July and $6.80 in the November," Gidel said. "It has to happen in the next two to three weeks. It might happen on the June 30 quarterly stocks report. If the report suggests we have less beans than we thought, it could be like last year with corn."
The USDA will release its quarterly stocks and crop production figures on June 30.
Last year, July corn futures surged to all-time highs above $5.00 a bushel after USDA in its June quarterly stocks report said old crop supplies were dangerously tight.
Dan Cekander, analyst with FIMAT Futures, said July soybeans could explode if USDA tinkers with old or new crop production figures on the quarterly stocks report.

"I think the jury is still out on the July," said Dan Cekander, analyst with FIMAT Futures. "The quarterly stocks number at the end of the month will be important. Confirming we've overstated 1996 production would get you back up there. The tight deliverable stocks situation might also do that."

Agrivisor Services analyst Dale Durchholz said July could face minor setbacks along the way but had little room to fall. He noted aggressive buying by China and others after prices fell to around $8.20 last week.
Soybean prices crumbled last week after Cargill Inc said it was importing South American soybeans.

"You don't have the ingredients in place at this point to trigger a major collapse in this market," Durchholz said. "The odds of a big rally have been diminished by last week's break but you can't totally rule it out."
